claims.text: Geometric overflow is a boundary violation of an admissible manifold under preserved internal coherence.
Geometric overflow represents a failure regime where LLM outputs remain fluent, internally stable, and high-confidence while violating externally defined constraints.
Boundary tension measures proximity to admissibility boundaries.
Boundary tension enables the detection of limit-state behavior preceding overflow.
Geometric overflow is orthogonal to calibration.
Perfectly calibrated models may exhibit coherent boundary crossing.
Overflow and collapse demonstrate regime separability in a retrieval-augmented question answering setting.

evidence.description: We define an admissible manifold induced by a structured family of constraints grounded in an external environment and formalize geometric overflow as boundary violation under preserved internal coherence.
This definition isolates a failure regime in which outputs remain fluent, internally stable, and high-confidence while violating externally defined constraints.
We further introduce boundary tension, a geometric quantity measuring proximity to admissibility boundaries and enabling detection of limit-state behavior preceding overflow.
We further introduce boundary tension, a geometric quantity measuring proximity to admissibility boundaries and enabling detection of limit-state behavior preceding overflow.
We prove that overflow is orthogonal to calibration: even perfectly calibrated models may exhibit coherent boundary crossing.

A minimal empirical illustration in a retrieval-augmented question answering setting demonstrates regime separability between overflow and collapse.

methodologies.name: Geometric Overflow and Boundary Tension Formalism
methodologies.description: A geometric framework using admissible manifolds induced by external constraints to define overflow and boundary tension.

limitations.text: Standard perspectives on hallucination (probabilistic miscalibration, distributional shift, generalization error) do not explicitly distinguish between internal representational instability and externally grounded boundary violations.
